keyVerseText: After this thing Jeroboam returned not from his evil way, but made again of the lowest of the people priests of the high places: whosoever would, he consecrated him, and he became one of the priests of the high places. made: Heb. returned and made consecrated: Heb. filled his hand
rootMeaning: The root of חָפֵץ (châphêts) conveys the idea of delighting or taking pleasure in something, with a literal sense of inclining toward or bending to what is desired. This Hebrew adjective expresses not only a simple wish or desire but an active pleasure and favor toward an object or action. The root thus enriches the English glosses by emphasizing an inward disposition of willing delight rather than mere preference.
usageInScripture: Throughout its eleven occurrences, חָפֵץ consistently carries the sense of delight, favor, or willing desire, as seen in translations like 'that favour,' 'whosoever would,' and 'that wish.' It appears in contexts describing both human and divine pleasure or willingness, highlighting a voluntary and heartfelt attitude. This range of usage reveals the word's flexibility to express both personal desire and God's disposition toward righteousness.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חָפֵץ deepens our grasp of how Scripture portrays the nature of desire and pleasure in relation to God and humanity. It reveals that God's favor is not arbitrary but rooted in His delight in righteousness, contrasting with His displeasure in wickedness. For believers, this word invites reflection on cultivating a willing and joyful heart aligned with God's will. It underscores the biblical call to desire what pleases God, fostering a faith that is both obedient and heartfelt.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 13:33, the phrase 'whosoever would' (חָפֵץ) emphasizes the open willingness or desire of the people to be consecrated as priests, despite the corrupt context. This word highlights the voluntary nature of their acceptance, underscoring a troubling readiness to conform to Jeroboam's illicit priesthood. Thus, חָפֵץ here conveys not just willingness but a deliberate choice that has spiritual consequences.
